name: Red Fort
story: Commissioned by Shah Jahan, the Red Fort anchored the new capital of Shahjahanabad. Its palaces, gardens and ceremonial spaces connect the walled city to the former riverfront. Read it alongside the streets and markets that grew around the imperial centre.

facts.label: Materials
facts.value: Red sandstone in walls and gates; marble in palaces

facts.label: Spatial system
facts.value: Gate, bazaar, audience halls, palaces and water channels

reading: Read the sequence from Lahori Gate through Chhatta Chowk to the audience halls. The eastern pavilions and water channels formed an intentional riverfront palace landscape.

name: Jama Masjid
story: Shah Jahan’s congregational mosque occupies an elevated position in the walled city. The large courtyard, gateways and surrounding lanes offer a useful reading of monument scale against the finer grain of Shahjahanabad.

facts.label: Construction
facts.value: 1650–1656 in the Ministry of Tourism account

facts.label: Principal spaces
facts.value: Raised gateways, large courtyard and domed prayer hall

reading: Study the elevated plinth and steps against the fine-grained surrounding streets. Published accounts differ on the construction chronology; the timeline follows the Ministry of Tourism account.

name: Fatehpuri Masjid
story: At the western end of Chandni Chowk, Fatehpuri Masjid forms a major spatial anchor opposite the Red Fort. Its setting is especially useful for studying the relationship between religious institutions, commercial streets and public space.
reading: Compare the building’s frontage, approach and open space with its surrounding street pattern. This is an editorial reading; detailed archival documentation remains to be verified.

name: Delhi Town Hall
story: The Town Hall introduced a colonial civic institution into the established fabric of Chandni Chowk. Its open foreground and formal frontage provide a contrasting urban condition within the dense commercial district.
reading: Compare the building’s frontage, approach and open space with its surrounding street pattern. This is an editorial reading; detailed archival documentation remains to be verified.

photo.author: Varun Shiv Kapur from New Delhi, India

name: Connaught Place
story: Designed as a commercial centre for New Delhi, Connaught Place uses concentric rings, radial streets and continuous colonnades. Compare its large, regular blocks with the smaller and less regular street network of Shahjahanabad.

sources.title: Wikipedia · Connaught Place
sources.checked: Legacy reference; not revalidated in this release

facts.label: Urban composition
facts.value: Concentric commercial rings and radial streets

reading: Compare the building’s frontage, approach and open space with its surrounding street pattern. This is an editorial reading; detailed archival documentation remains to be verified.

name: Jantar Mantar
story: Jai Singh II’s astronomical observatory turns measurement into architecture. Its masonry instruments occupy an open site within today’s central city, offering a distinctive contrast between scientific landscape and surrounding urban development.

facts.label: Form
facts.value: Large masonry instruments in an open compound

reading: Read each instrument as a piece of geometry designed for observation. Orientation and shadow are integral to its purpose, although this atlas does not simulate astronomical measurements.

name: Sacred Heart Cathedral
story: The cathedral is part of the institutional landscape of central New Delhi. Its formal approach, planted grounds and church building provide a counterpoint to the nearby commercial centre and government precincts.

sources.title: Wikipedia · Sacred Heart Cathedral
sources.checked: Legacy reference; not revalidated in this release

sources.title: Wikipedia · Sacred Heart Cathedral, New Delhi

facts.label: Construction milestone
facts.value: Began in 1930; sources describe different later completion milestones

reading: Compare the building’s frontage, approach and open space with its surrounding street pattern. This is an editorial reading; detailed archival documentation remains to be verified.

name: India Gate
story: A sandstone memorial arch designed by Edwin Lutyens commemorates Indian soldiers who died in the First World War and the Third Anglo-Afghan War. Its foundation stone was laid in 1921; the completed memorial was dedicated in 1931.
reading: Read the arch as a terminating landmark in the Central Vista landscape. Compare the ceremonial axis, traffic edges and large open lawns with the intimate street spaces of Old Delhi.

name: Humayun’s Tomb
story: A monumental garden tomb places a red-sandstone and marble mausoleum at the centre of a divided garden. Its Persian-influenced planning, arcaded plinth and double dome became important precedents for later Mughal funerary architecture.
reading: Compare the charbagh water axes, raised terrace and gateways. The garden and enclosing walls are part of the architectural composition; a building footprint alone cannot describe this landscape.

sources.title: UNESCO · Humayun’s Tomb
sources.checked: Further reading; portal unavailable during this refresh

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Garden axes, raised plinth, double dome and corner kiosks

name: Qutb Minar
story: The minaret developed through successive building campaigns, beginning under Qutb-ud-din Aibak and continuing under Iltutmish, with later repairs. Fluted shafts, inscriptions and projecting balconies make its construction history legible in the elevation.
reading: Study the tower together with the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque, Alai Darwaza and the Iron Pillar. The timeline marks the start of construction, not completion of every element of the complex.

facts.label: Patronage
facts.value: Aibak; additions by Iltutmish; subsequent repairs

facts.label: Materials
facts.value: Red and buff sandstone; marble in later portions

name: Lotus Temple
story: Fariborz Sahba’s House of Worship translates a lotus into a nine-sided architectural composition. Twenty-seven marble-clad petals form the outer image, while nine entrances connect the surrounding landscape to the central worship hall.
reading: Read the relationships between the petal groups, approach paths and nine reflecting pools. The footprint extrusion is schematic: it does not reproduce the curved shell structure.

name: Swaminarayan Akshardham
story: A contemporary temple campus on the east side of the Yamuna brings together a carved mandir, gardens and cultural exhibition spaces. Its visitor sequence extends far beyond the central shrine and makes landscape an essential part of the experience.
reading: Compare the central shrine, large processional paths and campus-scale edges. Use the cited operator guidance for current access rules; mapped entrances and building tags are not a visitor-access guarantee.

facts.label: Architectural character
facts.value: Carved stone mandir within a landscaped campus

name: Purana Qila
story: The Old Fort is associated with the building campaigns of Humayun and Sher Shah Suri. Gateways, defensive walls, the Qila-i Kuhna Mosque and Sher Mandal preserve different strands of that history within one enclosure.
reading: Study the enclosure, approach thresholds and the contrast between robust perimeter walls and freestanding internal structures. The date shown refers to the mosque, not the beginning of occupation of the site.

name: Agrasen ki Baoli
story: A long flight of steps descends between arcaded walls to a historic water structure on Hailey Road. Its origins and later rebuilding are uncertain; the Ministry of Tourism describes a likely medieval phase and distinguishes this from local legends.
reading: Read the site in section: descent, shade, water access and retaining walls are more informative here than a conventional above-ground extrusion. The timeline position is approximate.

name: Gurudwara Bangla Sahib
story: The gurdwara is associated with Guru Har Krishan’s stay in Delhi and service to people during illness. The present complex combines prayer, the sarovar and community facilities; the historical milestone does not date all its present buildings.
reading: Observe the relation between the prayer hall, water tank, shaded circulation and langar. These shared spaces help explain how an institution functions as part of the city.

sources.title: Ministry of Tourism · Gurudwara Bangla Sahib

facts.label: Principal spaces
facts.value: Prayer hall, sarovar and community kitchen

sourceName: Ministry of Tourism · Gurudwara Bangla Sahib

name: Lodhi Garden
story: Tombs from the Sayyid and Lodi periods sit within a later public landscape. The garden’s modern history includes its 1936 layout and a 1968 redesign associated with Garrett Eckbo and Joseph Allen Stein.
reading: Compare domed tombs, gateways, planting and walking routes. The time marker refers to Muhammad Shah’s tomb; the contemporary park is the result of many later interventions.

facts.label: Park phase
facts.value: Landscaped in 1936 as Lady Willingdon Park

facts.label: Later design
facts.value: 1968 changes by Garrett Eckbo and Joseph Allen Stein

facts.label: Study focus
facts.value: Heritage structures within everyday public open space

name: Raj Ghat
story: Raj Ghat marks the site of Mahatma Gandhi’s cremation on 31 January 1948. A restrained black-marble platform and a garden setting make a place of collective remembrance through deliberate simplicity.
reading: Look at procession, changes in level and the transition from the city into a contemplative landscape. The 1948 marker records the historical event rather than the completion of every landscape element.

photo.author: Humayunn Niaz Ahmed Peerzaada from Mumbai, India

name: National Museum
story: The National Museum on Janpath presents collections spanning archaeology, sculpture, painting and decorative arts. Established in 1949, the institution operates under the Ministry of Culture. The timeline dates the institution rather than all of its present buildings.
reading: Study the institutional frontage, approach and relationship to the government precinct. Use the museum website for current galleries and visiting arrangements, which can change independently of mapped geometry.

facts.label: Collections
facts.value: Archaeology, sculpture, paintings and decorative arts

name: National Gallery of Modern Art
story: The National Gallery of Modern Art occupies Jaipur House near India Gate and later exhibition buildings. The gallery traces Indian art from the mid-eighteenth century onward; the institution opened in 1954 and expanded with a new wing in 2009.
reading: Compare the historic domed house with the later gallery spaces and their courtyards. The 1954 marker dates the gallery’s establishment, not the original house.

sources.title: Ministry of Tourism · National Gallery of Modern Art

sourceName: Ministry of Tourism · National Gallery of Modern Art

name: National War Memorial
story: Beside India Gate, a landscape of concentric spaces honours armed-forces personnel who died in service after Independence. The design moves through circles of immortality, bravery, sacrifice and protection, using an obelisk, murals, inscribed walls and trees.
reading: Read the low landscape as a sequence of thresholds rather than a single object. Its relationship to the older India Gate makes the different commemorative histories visible.

sources.title: Ministry of Tourism · National War Memorial

facts.label: Composition
facts.value: Amar, Veerta, Tyag and Raksha Chakras

facts.label: Materials & elements
facts.value: Obelisk, bronze murals, inscribed granite walls and trees

facts.label: Landscape role
facts.value: A memorial precinct alongside India Gate

sourceName: Ministry of Tourism · National War Memorial

name: Safdarjung’s Tomb
story: Safdarjung’s Tomb is a late expression of the Mughal garden-tomb tradition. A prominent domed mausoleum, an elevated platform and an enclosed garden create an axial composition in the city south of the Central Vista.
reading: Compare its garden divisions and scale with Humayun’s Tomb. Inspect the hierarchy of the central tomb, gateway and subsidiary pavilions rather than treating the entire compound as one building.

facts.label: Spatial elements
facts.value: Central mausoleum, garden, gateway and pavilions

name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
story: Originally conceived as the Viceroy’s House, Rashtrapati Bhavan is now the residence of the President of India. Its domed mass, forecourt and gardens establish the western end of the Central Vista composition.
reading: Explore the relation of Raisina Hill, the ceremonial axis and the large estate. This is a building-history profile: public access is limited to authorised visitor circuits and bookings.

facts.label: Present role
facts.value: Residence of the President of India

facts.label: Design elements
facts.value: Central dome, forecourt, colonnades and gardens

name: Samvidhan Sadan (Old Parliament House)
story: The circular former Parliament House is a major component of New Delhi’s governmental ensemble. Designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker, it opened in 1927; its colonnaded perimeter distinguishes it from the axial government buildings nearby.
reading: Compare the circular plan, radial internal organisation and the open spaces around it. The linked Delhi Tourism account describes the historic Parliament House, not the newer Parliament building.

name: Hauz Khas Complex
story: The Hauz Khas complex places a madrasa and funerary architecture beside a historic reservoir. Water infrastructure, learning and commemoration meet in a setting that now borders an intensely used urban neighbourhood.
reading: Explore the reservoir edge, terraced buildings and transitions to the village streets. The fourteenth-century marker is approximate and applies to the madrasa phase rather than the original reservoir.

facts.label: Principal elements
facts.value: Reservoir, madrasa and Firoz Shah’s tomb
